glossary.definition: A Yale-built, web-based quality-control application that compares a draft pathology report against the patient's record — requisition, clinical notes, operative report, imaging, prior reports — before the report is finalized, and shows the pathologist what disagrees. In pilot since 2025; one click before sign-out.

A Yale specimen-custody application built in 2023–2025 after two spreadsheet-based tracking systems failed. Manifests travel with specimens between the operating room and the laboratory and stay open until the receiving party acknowledges them. Large language models helped write its specifications and code; none of them runs inside it.

Interactive Biomedical Inquiry System — an open-source search engine for anatomic pathology that turns a natural-language question into an inspectable Lucene query over structured and free-text case data, shows its interpretation and confidence, and waits for approval before executing. Built on synthetic data outside the institution.

An open-source generator of synthetic patient and staff records that sound like records, belong to nobody, and — in stress mode — include the values that break pipelines: empty strings, injection strings, diacritics, improbable dates. It establishes that a pipeline survives contact with data, not that the data are clinically plausible.

A keyboard-driven manual differential white-cell counter (also called the MDC), open source, with a full medical-device-style quality system: 71 user requirements, 207 system requirements, 56 hazards, 1,172 tests, and an append-only log of every claim that stopped being true.
Manual Differential Counter — the working name of WBC ΔΣ in the residents' lectures and in the repository's own code.

A Yale application (2012–) that links the operating room and the frozen-section area: the frozen-section diagnosis is entered once, sent to the OR for acknowledgement, and uploaded automatically to the laboratory information system.

Pathology Orders in Transit — a Yale application (2018–) that links the LIS with the EHR's ordering modules and tracks a specimen from the moment of biopsy or resection to its arrival in the laboratory.

Repetitive Task Scheduling Engine — Yale's workflow-orchestration engine (2007–), running the department's scheduled jobs: targeted reminders, clinical alerts, rare-event detection, system checks and data-integrity verification.
Rapidly Evolving Agile Laboratory Modules — the umbrella name for the assembly of small applications, on premises and in the cloud, that Yale Pathology Informatics runs alongside the commercial LIS.
Laboratory information system — the system of record for specimens, slides and reports. It records what happened. It rarely coordinates what must happen next.
Electronic health record — organized around encounters and orders rather than around what a pathologist needs to make a diagnosis.
Health Level Seven — the messaging standard through which laboratory and hospital systems exchange orders, results and documents. Exchange, not coordination.
The form that accompanies a specimen to the laboratory: who the patient is, what was taken, from where, and why. One of the documents a coherence check reads.
The surgeon's or proceduralist's account of what was done and what was seen. It may be dictated but unsigned when the specimen arrives.
Left or right. A laterality error in a report is one of the most consequential and most mechanical mistakes a document check can catch.

A pathology report corrected after release. Yale's 2014 study of 60 amended reports found that in seven cases the ordering and treating physicians differed, and the amendment reached the treating physician's chart in only one.

A disagreement between two statements about the same patient, specimen or finding. Which discrepancies matter — and which are only differences in wording — is a pathology question, not a programming detail.
An intraoperative consultation in which tissue is frozen, cut and read within minutes so the surgeon can act. The permanent section, read days later, is the reference against which it is scored.

Frozen-section quality assurance — the scoring of each frozen-section diagnosis against the permanent diagnosis, with the source of any discrepancy categorized and the discrepancy documented in the final report.
A required step the system will not let you skip. In the frozen-section QA program, scoring at sign-out became a hard stop six months after go-live.
Who has a specimen, where it is, and who has acknowledged receiving it — a chain that a spreadsheet can describe but cannot enforce.
A list of specimens travelling together from one location to another, created at the source and closed only when the receiving party acknowledges it.
The transfer of a specimen, a case or a task from one person or place to another. In most laboratory systems it is implicit; in an orchestrated one it has a state, an owner and a deadline.
A positive confirmation by the receiving party that something arrived. The difference between a message delivered and a step completed.
A layer that knows what must happen next in a workflow, who must do it, by when, and what to do when nobody does. Distinct from exchanging messages between systems.
Whether systems can coordinate the next step in the work, not merely exchange information about it. Asked as a practical question: who acts, who confirms, what happens when nobody does.
A model in which an object is always in exactly one named state and moves between states only through defined transitions. A handoff that must be acknowledged is a state machine with three states.
The part of a system whose behavior is fixed by its rules and tests rather than by a model's judgment. The place where routine operational decisions should live.

A model trained on text that can read, compare, summarize, translate and generate language and code. Inside an application it proposes; in a build pipeline it constructs. The two uses carry different evaluation burdens.

Software development in which an AI session plans, writes, runs and tests code toward a stated goal. Capable, thorough, and without memory of the previous session — which is why executable quality controls matter.
User requirements specification — what must be true, stated by the people who will use the system, each with a clinical rationale. The document only a domain expert can write.
System requirements specification — testable statements of system behavior derived from the user requirements.
Failure mode and effects analysis — a risk analysis that lists each way a system could fail, scores severity, occurrence and detectability, and names the control for each.
A table linking every requirement to the tests that verify it and the hazards it mitigates, in both directions. Only meaningful when it is generated from the artifacts rather than typed.
The international standard for medical-device software life-cycle processes: planning, requirements, architecture, verification, risk management and change control.
The controlled set of documents that records how a device was designed, verified and changed. For WBC ΔΣ it is public and inspectable.
Evidence that the software does what its requirements say. Verification against a copy of the implementation establishes nothing about the implementation that ships.
Evidence that the software serves its intended use in practice. A measured interval, a documented rate, a change in the work — not a demonstration.
A discipline for new tests: remove the fix, and the test must fail with the original symptom. Twice in the counter's history it found the test wrong before it found the code wrong.

The decay of a repository's statements about itself: documents, comments, procedures and counts that stop agreeing with the code and with each other. Acute when capable but stateless sessions do the work.
A quality management system whose controls run in the build — generated counts, consistency gates, provenance-stamped evidence — so that drift fails the build instead of waiting for a reviewer.
The rule that closing anything — a hazard, a gap, an open item — means touching everything that speaks about it. Closing without sweeping is how most drift incidents happened.

Records generated to resemble real ones without describing any real person. They let systems be built and tested outside the institution's security perimeter, and brought inside only along the governed pathway.
Xenonym's mode that deliberately generates the values that break systems — empty, oversized, injected, accented, improbable — so the pipeline meets them in a test rather than in production.
The declared shape of a record: which fields exist and what types they hold. A record that satisfies a schema has the right shape; nothing more is established.
The query language beneath Elasticsearch: fields, boolean operators, wildcards and ranges. IBIS translates a natural-language question into it and shows the result before running it.
Asking a database a question in ordinary language. The useful part is not the fluency of the answer but the inspectable query that sits between the question and the result.
The set of patients, specimens or reports that meets a definition. Which of the three units is being counted decides the number.
In IBIS, the step that shows the interpretation, the confidence, the extracted entities and the generated query, and waits for the user to approve before anything executes.
The small, accountable group between IT and the clinicians that hears a question, sharpens it, builds inside the security perimeter, verifies, and owns the artifact afterwards.
Something important, technically attainable, and absent from the vendor system — Gershkovich and Sinard, 2015. The place where custom infrastructure begins.
Protected health information. It never enters a prompt and never leaves the institution's perimeter; the systems in this talk were built on synthetic data for that reason.
The defined purpose a tool is validated for. A coherence check validated for laterality and site is not thereby validated for diagnosis.

The organizing idea of the earlier lectures in this series: when the cost of building collapses, the domain expert can articulate intent directly to working tools. This talk is about what that does to clinical practice.

James Reason’s picture of how systems fail: each defensive layer is a slice with holes that open, close and move; no single hole causes harm, and harm needs the holes in several layers to line up. BMJ 2000;320:768–770.

The Joint Commission’s term for a patient-safety event that results in death, permanent harm, or severe temporary harm. Wrong-surgery events were the second most frequently reported category in 2024, after falls.
A serious, largely preventable adverse event that should not occur if available safeguards are in place; wrong-site, wrong-patient and wrong-procedure surgery are the standard examples.

An operation on the wrong side, the wrong level or the wrong structure. In the Joint Commission’s review of 2024, 68% of wrong-surgery events were wrong-site, and incorrect laterality was cited in over half of those.

Whether a tissue specimen actually came from the patient whose name it carries. Occult provenance complications, switching and contamination, are measured by DNA comparison and were found in roughly one percent of prostate biopsies in a 2013 study.

Two forms of a claim about the future. A prophecy names an outcome and a date and gives no mechanism, so it cannot be checked until the date passes. A specification describes what a system would have to do, so it can be read backwards from its conclusion and checked step by step — and can be wrong in its particulars and still useful.

The two defect types that matter most in the Meier taxonomy of amended reports. A misinterpretation changes the diagnosis; a misidentification attaches a correct diagnosis to the wrong patient, specimen or site. With specimen defects and report defects they are the four categories of the CAP Q-Probes benchmark on the opening slide.

The College of American Pathologists’ voluntary, multi-institution quality benchmarking studies. The 2014 study of 73 institutions supplies the amended-report split on the opening slide; the 1998 study of 359 laboratories is the older benchmark.

The tendency to accept a machine’s output in place of one’s own check — Mukherjee’s parent whose child has spell-check and never learns to spell. The reason a coherence check asks the pathologist to decide and records the decision.

vizConfig.subtitle: Toronto, October 2016. The generous version of it expires this month.

lines: It’s just completely obvious that in five years deep learning is going to do better than radiologists.

quote.who: Geoffrey Hinton, to Siddhartha Mukherjee · The New Yorker, 3 April 2017 · on stage in Toronto, 27 October 2016

extension.text: In the future, learning algorithms will make pathological diagnoses.

vizConfig.thesis: The prediction aimed at the hardest thing and missed the easiest. Judgment is scarce, and the room knows it. Context is engineering — and nobody engineered it.

epigram.text: The algorithm can solve a case. It cannot build a case.

vizConfig.source: Mukherjee, The New Yorker 3 Apr 2017 · Creative Destruction Lab 27 Oct 2016 · NRMP 2026 Match · Lohr, NYT 14 May 2025 · Volmar et al, Arch Pathol Lab Med 2014

slides.speakerNotes: THE OPENING, about three minutes, two clicks. Read the quote and let the hedge sit; it is on the slide because it is fair. Attribution matters in this room: the lines are Hinton’s. Mukherjee carried them, and his own conclusion ran the other way, toward augmentation and the danger of automation bias. Do not argue with the person; argue with the form of the claim. A dated outcome with no mechanism cannot be read backwards and checked step by step. Bush and Licklider were wrong in most of their particulars and still useful, because they described mechanisms. You would never give a patient a prognosis with a date and no mechanism. Click: ten years later. The most diagnostic radiology positions in five years and nearly all of them filled; 636 pathology positions; the Mayo Clinic went from about 260 radiologists to more than 400; and in May 2025 the author of the prediction told the Times he had been wrong on the timing, not the direction, and had spoken only about image analysis. Click: what actually sends a report back. In the 2014 Q-Probes benchmark, one amended report in seven changed the interpretation; the taxonomy paper puts the fraction between a quarter and three in ten. Either way, most amendments are identification, specimen and report defects: a side, a part, a sentence that belongs to another case. The prediction aimed at judgment, the hardest thing, and missed context, the easiest. Judgment is scarce and the room knows it. Context is engineering, and nobody engineered it. That sentence is the talk. If you have split the department’s own amendments by the same taxonomy, put the department’s numbers here in place of the benchmark; it is the strongest slide you can show. Two places a hostile listener will stand: wrong-site surgery is mostly an operating-room process failure, so keep the pathology version narrow, the amendment that arrives after the surgery because the side on the report was wrong; and define the missing component by what Dialogue needed that the model did not supply: reading the case before sign-out, sitting at the right point in the workflow, and a record of what it caught.

takeaway.text: The 2016 prediction aimed at judgment. What sends a report back is mostly context: identification, specimen and report defects. Judgment is scarce; context is engineering.
takeaway.comment: Prophecy against specification. The quarrel is with the form of the claim, not the person: a dated outcome with no mechanism cannot be read backwards and checked step by step, and the hedge stays on the slide because it was fairly made. Everything this hour claims is stated as a mechanism — what it took to build, what it caught, what most places still lack — and carries no date.

slides.speakerNotes: OPTIONAL, one minute. The anxiety you remember in the residents’ room was measured. Canada, 2018: one in six students who would have ranked radiology first would not, because of AI; nearly half of the first-choice students called it a source of anxiety. The United Kingdom a year later: 49% of 484 students less likely to consider radiology. The United States in 2020: one in six again. The prediction had a measurable cost years before it had a measurable benefit. Then the author’s own revision in 2025. No commentary needed; the four numbers do the work. Cut this slide first if the hour is tight. The 2025 quotation is as reported by AuntMinnie and The Decoder from Lohr’s Times piece of 14 May 2025; the Times text itself was not checked, so present it as reported.

takeaway.text: The prediction had a measurable cost years before it had a measurable benefit.
takeaway.comment: Three surveys of medical students, 2018 to 2020 — Gong (Canada), Sit (United Kingdom), Reeder and Lee (United States) — asked the same question and got the same answer: students who would have chosen radiology were turning away because of AI, one in six in Canada and the United States, nearly half less likely in the United Kingdom. The prediction did not have to be right to have an effect. It had to be heard by people choosing a specialty, and it was heard years before its author revised it.

slides.dockTitle: A case, not an architecture diagram

vizConfig.title: What does not agree?
vizConfig.subtitle: Three cases, three documents each. Read them the way you would at sign-out, before anything is highlighted.
vizConfig.prompt: Before anything is revealed: what does not agree — and which of the differences would you act on?
vizConfig.summary: Three kinds of disagreement: side, plausibility, completeness. Three differences in wording that were not errors. Telling them apart is a pathology question — and it is where this hour begins.

cases.label: Breast core biopsy

lines.text: 62-year-old woman. Screening mammogram: 1.2 cm spiculated mass, BI-RADS 4.
Specimen: LEFT breast, 10 o’clock, ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy.
Clinical question: rule out carcinoma.
Three cores submitted in formalin.
Procedure: ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the left breast mass at 10 o’clock, 4 cm from the nipple.
Findings: hypoechoic 1.2 cm lesion corresponding to the mammographic abnormality.
Three core samples obtained; a marker clip was placed; specimen sent to pathology.
RIGHT BREAST, 10 O’CLOCK, CORE NEEDLE BIOPSY:
Invasive ductal carcinoma, Nottingham grade 2.
Ductal carcinoma in situ, intermediate grade, present.
Tumor measures at least 0.9 cm in the cores. See synoptic report.

flag.label: System flag
flag.title: Laterality disagrees between the draft report and both source documents.
lines: Requisition: LEFT breast, 10 o’clock · Operative note: left breast, 10 o’clock · Draft report: RIGHT BREAST, 10 O’CLOCK.
Core count is expressed differently (three cores / three core samples) but does not conflict. Not raised.

decision.label: Pathologist decision
options: Accept the flag; correct the header before release
Dismiss, with a reason the system will learn from
Open the three source documents side by side

cases.lesson: Side. The diagnosis is right and the record is wrong — and everything downstream reads the header, not the histology.

cases.label: Prostate biopsy

lines.text: 30-year-old man. PSA 8.4 ng/mL.
MRI: PI-RADS 4 lesion, left peripheral zone, 1.1 cm.
Specimen: MRI-targeted cores, left (3), and systematic cores (12).
Clinical question: rule out carcinoma.
30 M with rising PSA, 4.1 → 8.4 ng/mL over 18 months.
Target: left PZ, 1.1 cm, PI-RADS 4.
MRI-US fusion biopsy: 3 targeted cores and 12 systematic cores. Tolerated well; results in clinic.
A. PROSTATE, LEFT PERIPHERAL ZONE, TARGETED CORES:
Prostatic adenocarcinoma, Gleason score 3+4=7 (Grade Group 2), in 2 of 3 cores, up to 40% of core length.
B. PROSTATE, SYSTEMATIC CORES: Benign prostatic tissue in 12 of 12 cores.
Perineural invasion: not identified.

flag.label: System flag
flag.title: The documents agree — and the diagnosis is exceptional for the stated age.
lines: Requisition and urology note both give the age as 30. Grade Group 2 adenocarcinoma at 30 is rare enough that a registration or labeling error is the likelier explanation.
Verify identity and date of birth against the registration record before release. Left PZ and left peripheral zone are the same thing. Not raised.

decision.label: Pathologist decision
options: Check the date of birth and MRN against the registration record
Age confirmed: release, with a comment on the unusual age
Dismiss the flag, with a reason

cases.lesson: Plausibility. Nothing disagreed. Agreement among documents is not a record that makes sense — and this check needs what a pathologist knows.

cases.label: Colon biopsies

lines.text: 58-year-old woman. Screening colonoscopy. Two containers received.
A: Sigmoid colon, polyp, snare polypectomy.
B: Cecum, cold biopsies × 3, patchy erythema.
1.2 cm pedunculated polyp in the sigmoid colon, snared and retrieved — container A.
Patchy erythema in the cecum; three cold biopsies — container B.
Withdrawal time 9 minutes; preparation adequate.
A. COLON, SIGMOID, POLYPECTOMY: Tubular adenoma with low-grade dysplasia. Negative for high-grade dysplasia or malignancy.
Gross: a 1.2 cm polyp on a stalk, bisected and entirely submitted.
Comment: Clinical correlation with the mammographic findings is recommended.

flag.label: System flag
flag.title: Two things: Part B was received and is not reported, and one sentence belongs to another case.
lines: Requisition and endoscopy note both record container B (cecum, biopsies × 3); the draft reports Part A only.
“Clinical correlation with the mammographic findings” in a colon case is a copy-and-paste remnant. Pedunculated and on a stalk are the same thing. Not raised.

decision.label: Pathologist decision
options: Open the case: was Part B grossed, embedded and sectioned?
Delete the remnant sentence and re-read the comment

cases.lesson: Completeness and remnants. What was received must be answered; what was pasted must be read — these are the errors amendments are made of.

slides.speakerNotes: THE CASES, right after the prediction: three cases, about four minutes. The prediction aimed at judgment; here is what actually goes wrong. Case 1: say nothing for ten seconds; let the room read; ask what does not agree. Someone finds the side. Click: the laterality lines turn crimson and an amber pair appears, three cores against three core samples. Ask which of the two they would act on; that is the first lesson, which contradictions matter is a pathology question. Click for the flag, click for the decision, which is the pathologist’s. Click for case 2 and ask the same question. Nothing disagrees. Let the silence run; someone will say the age. A Grade Group 2 adenocarcinoma in a 30-year-old whose requisition and urology note both say 30 is not a document mismatch, it is an implausibility, and the likeliest explanation is a registration error that propagated into every document. This is the check that needs what a pathologist knows. Case 3: Part B was received, accessioned, and never reported, and the comment recommends mammographic correlation in a colon case. Two flags, one of them the error that amendments are made of. The closing line ties the three together: side, plausibility, completeness, and three wording differences that were not errors. All cases are synthetic; the banner says so. The breast case mirrors a real October 2025 catch at Yale.

takeaway.text: A correct diagnosis is not the same as a coherent clinical record.
takeaway.comment: Every diagnosis in the three drafts is right, and every record has a defect the slide cannot show: a side, an age the diagnosis does not fit, a container that was received and never reported, a sentence pasted from another case. Everything downstream — the surgeon, the tumor board — reads the header, the age and the comment, not the histology. This hour is not about whether AI can recognize cancer. It is about another layer of scrutiny over the relationships that make a diagnosis clinically usable.

vizConfig.title: This is not hypothetical.
vizConfig.subtitle: Documented cases in which the record, not the histology, was wrong — and what finally caught it.

cases.confused: Two women’s breast biopsy samples mislabeled at a reference laboratory; the state health department traced it to one technician’s labeling.
cases.happened: A 35-year-old had a double mastectomy for a cancer she did not have. The other woman was told she had none.
cases.caught: After the surgery, when the laboratory’s error came to light.

cases.confused: The wrong kidney was listed as cancerous on the chart weeks before surgery; every later step followed the chart.
cases.happened: The healthy kidney was removed from a cancer patient. The hospital accepted full responsibility.
cases.caught: After the operation. The surgical safety steps had all been followed.

cases.confused: Two men’s prostate biopsies confused at a private pathology laboratory.
cases.happened: One, 60, had a prostatectomy for a cancer he did not have. The other, 53, was told he was clear; eight months later his cancer had reached a lymph node.
cases.caught: A second biopsy at a different laboratory, and a disclosure letter admitting the slides were mixed up.

cases.confused: The eighth rib carried a precancerous lesion and had been marked with metal coils and dye. The seventh was removed.
cases.happened: A second operation the same day, and a lawsuit over what the patient was told afterwards.
cases.caught: A post-operative X-ray: the markers were still in place.

cases.confused: Another patient’s endometrial biopsy labeled as hers, the lawsuit alleges; how is still unclear.
cases.happened: A hysterectomy at 43 for an aggressive cancer that DNA analysis later showed was not hers.
cases.caught: A DNA analysis, four months after surgery. Lawsuit filed August 2026; allegations unproven.

cases.confused: The right leg was marked for amputation. The left was amputated.
cases.happened: A 74-year-old veteran became a double amputee when the intended surgery followed four months later. The hospital called it an “avoidable event”.
cases.caught: The team realized during the procedure.

vizConfig.caption: Every one was caught by a layer nobody had designed as a check: the pathology of what was removed, a post-operative X-ray, a second biopsy, a DNA test.

slides.speakerNotes: Six cases, all public, none of them about the microscope. In every one the histology was read correctly and the record around it was wrong: a label, a chart entry, a side, a container. Long Island 2007: two biopsies swapped at a reference lab; a double mastectomy for a cancer that belonged to someone else. St. Louis Park 2008: the wrong kidney listed as cancerous on the chart weeks before surgery, and every later step followed the chart; the hospital said the safety steps had been followed, which is the point. Boston 2010: two men’s prostate biopsies confused; one lost a prostate he did not need to lose, the other’s cancer reached a node while he was told he was clear. New Haven 2015, our own town: the rib was marked with coils and dye and the wrong one came out; the post-operative X-ray caught it. Georgia 2025: a hysterectomy at 43 for a cancer that DNA testing later said was not hers; a lawsuit, allegations unproven, say so. Ohio 2025: the right leg marked, the left amputated; included because the marking was right and the layers still failed. Then the scale: 127 wrong-surgery events reported to the Joint Commission last year, up for the third year running, laterality in over half of the wrong-site cases; four identification errors per thousand surgical specimens at one academic center; a quarter of a percent of prostate biopsies switched between patients. And the sentence on the caption: every one of these was caught by a layer nobody had designed as a check. Pfeifer and Liu’s data came from Strand Analytical Laboratories, which markets the DNA test; say so if asked.

takeaway.text: Every one of these was caught by a layer nobody had designed as a check. The histology was right; the record was wrong.
takeaway.comment: Six public cases from 2007 to 2025, none of them about the microscope. In each the histology was read correctly and the record around it was wrong — a label, a chart entry, a side, a container — and the error was found by something that happened to lie downstream: the pathology of what was removed, a post-operative X-ray, a second biopsy, a DNA test. The scale is from the Joint Commission’s review of 2024 and three published series; the prostate-biopsy figures rest on data supplied by a laboratory that sells the DNA test.

vizConfig.title: Why they get through.
vizConfig.subtitle: Every layer has holes, and each layer assumes the one before it checked. Click to put a layer that reads across the documents in before release.

layers.label: Registration and requisition
layers.hole: age typed as 30; the side typed from memory

layers.label: Accessioning
layers.hole: two containers received, one part logged

layers.label: Grossing
layers.hole: the side copied from the requisition

layers.label: Histology
layers.hole: blocks and slides labeled from the cassette

layers.label: Sign-out
layers.hole: the diagnosis is right; the header is not re-read

layers.label: Report release
layers.hole: the EHR takes what it is given

layers.label: Surgeon and tumor board
layers.hole: the header is what gets read

inserted.label: Coherence check
inserted.note: reads across the documents; holes of its own: what is not in the record, what it reads wrong

quote.text: Reason’s picture: the defences of a system are slices of Swiss cheese, each with holes that open, close and move. No single hole causes harm. Harm needs the holes to line up.
quote.who: after Reason J, Human error: models and management. BMJ 2000;320:768–770

vizConfig.caption: The inserted layer is not a slice without holes. It is a slice with different holes — which is why the pathologist’s decision stays.

slides.speakerNotes: James Reason’s model, drawn for our own process. Seven layers between the clinic and the surgeon, and every one has holes: the age typed wrong at registration, the second container never logged, the side copied from the requisition at the grossing bench, the cassette label trusted at the microtome, the header not re-read at sign-out, the EHR taking what it is given, the surgeon reading the header. Watch the line. One error, and every layer assumes the layer before it checked. Nobody noticed, because noticing was nobody’s step. Click. A layer that reads across the documents goes in before release. Look at where its holes are: not on the line. It cannot see what is not in the record, and it will sometimes read wrong, which is exactly why the flag goes to a pathologist and does not close the case by itself. The model is an argument for a different slice, not for a perfect one.

takeaway.text: Each layer assumes the one before it checked. A coherence check is a slice with different holes, not a slice without holes.
takeaway.comment: After Reason J, BMJ 2000;320:768–770, paraphrased. Reason’s person approach asks who mislabeled the specimen; his system approach asks why no later layer could see it. Every layer in a pathology case was built to catch its own class of error and inherits whatever the layer before it passed on. A check that reads across the documents is one more slice with its own holes — what is not in the record, what it misreads — which is why the flag goes to a pathologist and does not close the case by itself.

slides.title: A Different Question
slides.subtitle: Most of the AI conversation in pathology asks one thing. This hour asks another.

left.heading: The Usual Question
bullets: Can a computer recognize what we recognize on a slide?
Models, benchmarks, AUROC — the computer as a reader
The pathologist as a user of whatever is delivered
Progress measured by what the model can do

slides.speakerNotes: Much of the discussion about AI in pathology asks whether a computer can recognize what we recognize on a slide. Today I want to ask a different question: what happens when we can translate our knowledge of how pathology should work into systems that actually work that way? Three working systems from one department will carry the argument — one clinical, one operational, one research — and then a fourth, the smallest, will answer the objection the first three provoke. This is the sentence the room should leave with. Say it once here, once at the end, and not in between.

takeaway.text: Modern AI is changing not only what computers can do for pathologists, but what pathologists can make their systems do.
takeaway.comment: Two readings of “AI in pathology”. The usual one asks what a model can recognize on a slide, which is a question about capability, answered with benchmarks. Today’s asks what a pathologist can now get a system to do — specify it, build it, test it, revise it — which is a question about infrastructure, answered with working systems. The three that follow are from one department; the fourth answers the objection they provoke.

A model that proposes inside an application — you evaluate it, you decide — from a model that helps build an application that then runs without it.
Which of five claims a system makes — it runs, its tests pass, it meets its requirements, it changed practice, patients did better — and what would prove each, whoever built it.
One page for one recurring problem: what the system should do, what it must never do, what evidence would convince you — the one part of this work nobody can do for you.

The second is the next slide, and it asks each of you for one workaround. The third is the distinction that stops the word AI from explaining everything. The fourth is what to ask of any system, including ours. The fifth is the assignment. Say it plainly: nobody in this room is being asked to program. You are being asked to say what the system should do, what it must never do, and what would convince you — and that is the part nobody else can write.

slides.title: Three Questions From an Ordinary Week

epigraph.text: Recognizing what should happen is not the same as having infrastructure that makes it happen.

items.question: Why can't the system check whether these documents describe the same clinical story?
items.detail: Clinical. The requisition, the operative note, the imaging, the prior reports and the draft all describe one patient. Today the reconciliation happens in the pathologist's head, under time pressure, and nothing records that it happened.

items.question: Why can't we make the specimen-handling process work the way we know it should?
items.detail: Operational. A specimen leaves the operating room and arrives in the laboratory — or does not. Twice, a spreadsheet stood in for a system. Nothing in a spreadsheet can insist that someone acknowledge receipt.

items.question: Why can't I turn this clinical question into a reproducible search of our own experience?
items.detail: Research. The observation at sign-out — we seem to be seeing more of these — dies in the analyst queue, or becomes a different question that the data happened to be able to answer.

items.question: Why do I still compensate for all of this by hand?
items.detail: All three. Because changing the software seemed harder than living with the problem. That was an economic fact, not a technical one — and it is the fact that has changed.

slides.speakerNotes: Hover each question: the detail names the compensation pathologists make today. These are three manifestations of the same problem. Recognizing what should happen is not the same as having infrastructure that makes it happen. The fourth question is the honest one, and the next slide is about why its answer changed. Do not let the room hear this as a complaint about vendors; the distance was rational, and the argument is that the cost moved.

takeaway.text: Three manifestations of one distance: between knowing what should happen and having infrastructure that makes it happen.
takeaway.comment: This is not a complaint about vendors. The distance was rational: for twenty years, closing it cost more than the problem was worth — a software project, a budget line, a vendor queue — so every department compensated by hand and called it workflow. The argument of the hour is that the cost moved, not that anyone was wrong.

The check has to run before release, because amendments do not follow the patient. And nobody is accountable for a machine’s opinion unless a pathologist decides. The right-hand column is what Dialogue does about each one, and every item is a design decision, not a model property. Name the missing component the way you would in a hallway: AI engineering — reading the case before sign-out, sitting at the right point in the workflow, and a record of what it caught. takeaway.text: The capability is not the hard part. The missing component is engineering — assembly, perimeter, noise, timing and accountability — and each is a design decision.

Reading is no longer the bottleneck. Everything on the left is — assembly, free text, the perimeter, noise, timing, accountability — and every answer on the right is a design decision, not a model property. Some of Dialogue’s flag classes are live in the pilot; the rest are by design, and the slide says which.

cards.label: Ordering vs. treating physician

cards.label: Reached the treating chart

slides.speakerNotes: Why prevention rather than a better amendment workflow. In 2014 we followed sixty amended reports. In seven the ordering and treating physicians were different people — all malignant diagnoses — and the amended report was in the treating physician's chart in exactly one. No harm was documented, and neither EHR had any way to alert the team. Amendments do not reliably follow the patient. Then the 2025 account: a laterality error caught before release, nine months from concept to usable tool, feedback and rating built in. And the sixth card, which I want on the slide rather than in my mouth: not yet validated. Nothing has been published about sensitivity, specificity or the amendment rate. The 2025 Yale news article names the developers and the catch but gives no counts.

takeaway.text: Amended reports do not reliably follow the patient. Preventing the error before release is worth more than any amendment workflow.
takeaway.comment: Parkash and colleagues, Am J Clin Pathol 2014;142:58–63, followed sixty amended reports to the physician responsible for the patient. In seven cases the ordering and treating physicians differed; the amended report was in the treating chart in one, and neither EHR could alert the team. An amendment is issued; whether it reaches the person treating the patient is another matter. Hence prevention before release rather than a better amendment workflow. The 2025 account of Dialogue’s first catch reports the catch, not a rate.

slides.title: The Questions That Require Your Expertise

left.heading: What the System Can Be Made to Do

Ignore wording differences that do not change the diagnosis

Improve from your ratings

right.heading: What Only a Pathologist Can Decide

Whether the diagnosis is plausible for this patient — and if not, whether the error is in the diagnosis or in the identity
What information was actually available to the system when it flagged, or failed to flag
What you should see before accepting or dismissing a flag
When the system should ask for clarification rather than proceed

slides.speakerNotes: This is the intellectual tension of the hour, and it is the reason a grand-rounds audience is the right one. When implementation gets cheap, defining the right behavior gets more important, not less. What counts as a discrepancy? Three cores against three core samples is not one; left against right is. Is a Grade Group 2 adenocarcinoma plausible at 30, and if not, is the error in the slide or in the wristband? What information did the system actually have: was the operative note signed yet? What should you see before you dismiss a flag, the system’s reading or the source lines? When should it stop and ask? These are substantive pathology questions. The programming is the easy part now. If there is time, ask the room for one more item for the right-hand column. There is always one, and it is usually better than mine.

takeaway.text: What counts as a discrepancy is a substantive pathology question, not a programming detail.
takeaway.comment: The right-hand column is never finished, and every item on it is a judgment before it is a rule. Whether a Grade Group 2 adenocarcinoma at thirty is implausible or merely unusual, whether a missing part is an omission or a decision, whether a pasted sentence is a shortcut or an error — each is something only a pathologist can decide, and once written down it becomes a specification a system can be tested against.

vizConfig.title: A handoff is not complete because somebody typed a destination.
vizConfig.subtitle: Specimen custody between the operating room and intake — the moment clinical intent becomes something a system can enforce and audit.

left.heading: The spreadsheet version

right.heading: The Hedgehog version

cards.text: Specimens went missing between the operating room and pathology intake. Ad-hoc, Excel-based tracking failed twice: nothing enforced a consistent workflow, so custody had gaps.
A handoff is not complete merely because somebody entered a destination. The receiving party must acknowledge receipt, and an open handoff stays visible until they do.
A manifest is created at the source, travels with the specimens, and remains open and visible to both ends until the receiver acknowledges it by name.
Given a manifest sent and not acknowledged within the threshold, the system must alert the sender and the receiving location — and the test fails if it does not.

vizConfig.caption: Large language models contributed to the requirements, the architecture, the code and the security review of Hedgehog. None of them decides, at runtime, whether a specimen has arrived.

slides.speakerNotes: The first important turn of the talk: AI does not have to make a clinical decision to change clinical care. It can help us build the system that makes the intended workflow possible. Hedgehog exists because specimens went missing and two spreadsheets failed. The spreadsheet version, on the left, has a gap drawn into it: a destination typed, nobody asked to confirm. The Hedgehog version has a transition called acknowledge and a guard under it. The audience does not need a code tour. It needs to see where the laboratory's knowledge changed the design — the requirement card, which I have labelled illustrative because it is my formulation of the rule, not a quotation from a document. Problem, requirement, behavior, test. That is the translation, and it is the same four cards for every system in this talk. No usage statistics are published; claim none.

takeaway.text: AI does not have to make a clinical decision to change clinical care. It can help build the system that makes the intended workflow possible.
takeaway.comment: Hedgehog was built between 2023 and 2025 after two Excel-based tracking systems failed. Language models turned stated goals into formatted specifications, critiqued the architecture, generated working frameworks within hours and challenged the developers on security. At runtime no model is involved: a manifest is open or acknowledged, and nothing probabilistic decides which. No usage statistics are published, and the slide claims none.

vizConfig.banner: These are infrastructure and workflow results — not evidence of an AI effect. The software predates the AI-assisted era. What AI changes is how fast such infrastructure can be built, tested and revised.

slides.speakerNotes: Real numbers from our own laboratory, published this year. Frozen-section QA built into sign-out: scoring at the moment of sign-out, a reason required for disagreement, automated e-mail to the frozen-section pathologist, a weekly review module, and after six months a hard stop. Mean time from frozen section to QA scoring: seventy days to eight. Discrepancies documented in the final report: thirty-five percent to seventy-five. The discrepancy rate itself went from 3.2 to 2.2 percent and that was not significant, and it is drawn dashed so nobody has to take my word for it. Now the sentence in the crimson box. These are infrastructure and workflow results. They are not evidence of an AI effect, and anyone who tells you otherwise about their own numbers is confusing two clocks. We already knew that changing infrastructure changes practice. The new question is how AI-assisted engineering changes our ability to build, test and revise it.

takeaway.text: We already knew that changing infrastructure changes practice. The question now is how AI-assisted engineering changes our ability to build, test and revise it.
takeaway.comment: Gibson, Mutnick, Gershkovich and Sinard, Am J Clin Pathol 2025;163:794–802. The program is ordinary infrastructure, none of it AI: FSLink, a scoring module inside CoPath (agree, margin assurance, defer, disagree with a reason), an automated e-mail to the frozen-section pathologist, a weekly review module and a quarterly M&M conference. Build the intended workflow into sign-out and practice follows — seventy days to eight. What AI changes is how quickly such a program can be built, tested and revised.

left.heading: Exchange
left.note: Every spoke receives a copy of the same message. Nobody owns what must happen next, who must acknowledge it, or when silence becomes a problem.

right.heading: Coordinate

what to do when nobody does
right.note: FSLink sends the frozen-section diagnosis to the OR and waits for acknowledgement; POinT follows orders in transit; Hedgehog holds custody open; RTSE runs the reminders. Twenty years of one department's answer to the question.

vizConfig.caption: Standards that describe the container are necessary. The laboratory's problem is the contract around it: who acts, who confirms, and what happens when nobody does.

slides.speakerNotes: The interoperability argument, introduced as a practical question rather than as standards terminology. On the left, exchange: the LIS sends a message and everybody gets a copy. On the right, a layer that holds state — what must happen next, who must acknowledge, what to do when nobody does — and the systems that have been doing this at Yale for years: FSLink waiting for the OR to acknowledge a frozen-section diagnosis, POinT following an order in transit, Hedgehog holding custody open, RTSE running the reminders and rare-event detection. The fur-coat paper makes the long version of this argument. The short version is on the caption. The FSLink acknowledgement step is described in the AJCP 2025 frozen-section paper.

takeaway.text: Exchanging a message is not the same as coordinating the next step. The second is what the laboratory actually needs.
takeaway.comment: Gershkovich P. Wearing a fur coat in the summertime: should digital pathology redefine medical imaging? J Pathol Inform 2025;18:100450. A message tells the next system that something happened. Coordination tells the next person what to do about it, by when, and what happens if they do not — and keeps the record that they did. FSLink is the smallest example: a frozen-section diagnosis sent to the operating room waits for acknowledgement, and silence becomes an event rather than an absence. Standards describe the envelope; the laboratory’s problem is the contract.

The unit is yours to decide. Patients, specimens, or reports; final diagnosis or clinical history; amendments and repeats — the vendor’s data model used to answer these for you, silently.
The artifact is reproducible. The generated query goes in the methods section; a reviewer can re-run it against the same archive.

slides.title: The Objection: You Can Build This Quickly. How Do You Know It Behaves Correctly?
slides.subtitle: The smallest clinical application in the portfolio carries the largest quality system — mdc.openpathology.org · OpenPathologyFoundation/tessera

slides.speakerNotes: The objection the first three systems should provoke: you can build this quickly; how do you know it behaves correctly? I will answer with the smallest application I have. A manual differential counter — press a key, the count goes up. Seventy-one user requirements, two hundred and seven system requirements, fifty-six hazards, eleven hundred and seventy-two tests, one hundred percent traceability. Every artifact is in a public repository. It is simple on purpose. The safety envelope around it is the part worth studying — and the next two slides are about where that envelope failed before it held. Counts are the README’s generated qms:fact fields at v2.24.0 (23 Aug 2026). The residents’ lecture quoted 156 tests and 47 requirements; those were true in February 2026 and are superseded. Say so if a resident remembers.

takeaway.text: The application is simple on purpose. The safety envelope around it is the part worth studying — including where it failed.
takeaway.comment: The counts are the counter’s own, generated from its quality-management records at version 2.24.0 (23 August 2026) rather than typed, because typed counts drifted. They have grown since this material was first shown in February 2026, when there were 156 tests and 47 requirements. An application this simple exists to make the envelope around it legible: requirements with a clinical rationale, hazards traced to controls, tests that execute the shipped code, and a public record of where all of that failed first.

slides.speakerNotes: Here is the revealing failure, and it is mine. The v2.0 baseline: three hundred and seventy-nine tests, one hundred percent passing, every one of these green squares. Click. Zero of them executed the application. Half re-implemented the algorithms inside the test file and verified the copy; the rest checked that the source code contained certain strings. Click again. Fourteen real defects sat behind that green build: export buttons wired to nothing, percentages that never summed to a hundred, user input reaching a clinical report unescaped, formula injection in the CSV export. The suite that certified the build could not have caught any of them. On the right, what it took: three layers that execute the shipped code, in three browsers, and two rules — no layer verifies a copy, and every new test is revert-checked. A system that passes a test is not the same as a system whose tests execute it. This is the failure mode that AI-assisted development makes cheap, and it is why the next slide exists. If challenged on 379: it is from DCR-004 §1; TR-001’s comparison table records 191 at the same baseline. The point survives either number.

takeaway.text: A system that passes a test is not the same as a system whose tests execute it. Verification theater is the failure mode AI makes cheap.
takeaway.comment: The 379 figure is from the project’s own change record (DCR-004); a later technical report counts 191 tests at the same baseline. The argument survives either number: none of them executed the application. A green build is a statement about the tests, not about the software. It becomes a statement about the software only when the tests are shown to reach it — which is what the two rules on the right enforce, and what revert-checking proved twice by finding the test wrong before the code.

slides.speakerNotes: Fifty-two incidents in which the repository asserted something that had stopped being true, logged append-only, forty-two now prevented by a check that fails the build. The headline: the operating procedure said press A for blasts; the shipped layout had A as monocytes. Nobody wrote a false sentence. The layout changed, correctly, with tests, and the procedure was not swept. In a hematology laboratory the distance between blasts and monocytes is the distance between leukemia and a normal marrow. The taxonomy: counts kept by hand, two writers for one fact, closures not swept, versions advanced in one place, evidence without provenance — and one row, in crimson, still unguarded. What fixed it was not a better model. The quality system had existed from the start, as prose, and caught nothing. It started catching things when it became code.

takeaway.text: The quality system caught nothing while it was prose. It started catching things when it became code that fails the build.
takeaway.comment: The transferable lesson: treat AI sessions as capable staff who rotate every conversation, and give them what regulated laboratories learned to give rotating staff — document control, change records, a closure checklist, and verification that depends on nobody’s memory. Nothing here was careless; each session answered the question it was asked and never asked what else says this. None of it requires a medical context, and all of it is cheaper than the incident it prevents.

slides.title: Xenonym — The Records That Break Pipelines
slides.subtitle: Live at xenonym.openpathology.org — synthetic test cases in a realistic mode and a stress mode
slides.speakerNotes: Sixty seconds. Every system in this talk was built on synthetic data outside the institution. Xenonym is where the test cases come from: names that sound like names and belong to nobody, and in stress mode, the ones that break pipelines — the empty string, the injection string, the diacritics, the improbable date. Say what it establishes and what it does not. A schema-conforming synthetic record proves your pipeline accepts the shape. It does not prove the record is clinically plausible, and it is not a privacy guarantee. The next harness to build is the one Dialogue needs: records that are individually valid and mutually inconsistent. Xenonym has no cross-record consistency feature; do not claim one.

takeaway.text: Schema-conforming synthetic data establish neither clinical validity nor a privacy guarantee. They establish that your pipeline survives contact with data.
takeaway.comment: Xenonym generates records that are each valid against the schema, including the ones that break pipelines; it has no notion of consistency between records. The test set Dialogue actually needs — records individually valid and mutually inconsistent, a requisition that says left and a note that says right — is the obvious next tool, and it is exactly the kind of supplementary infrastructure that has become affordable to build.

slides.dockTitle: Five claims, five kinds of evidence

vizConfig.title: A record that satisfies a schema. A system that passes a test. A capability validated in use.
vizConfig.subtitle: Five claims, five kinds of evidence — and where each of the four systems honestly sits.

rungs.claim: The data has the right shape
rungs.evidence: Xenonym stress mode: names that sound like names, belong to nobody, and include the ones that break pipelines. Establishes that the pipeline accepts the shape — not that the record is clinically plausible, or private.

rungs.evidence: WBC ΔΣ: 1,172 tests, 0 failures. Meaningful only because no layer verifies a copy and every new test is revert-checked — the 379 that executed nothing passed too.

Not yet established for any of the four. The discrepancy rate fell from 3.2% to 2.2% and was not significant; no amendment-rate effect for Dialogue has been measured. The rung stays empty until it is.

verbs.detail: the shipped code, not a copy

vizConfig.caption: Faster construction makes explicit requirements, expert review and good tests more valuable, not less. The ladder is how you say which claim you are making.

slides.speakerNotes: Five claims, five kinds of evidence. A record that satisfies a schema — Xenonym. A system that passes a test — the counter, and only because the tests execute the shipped code. A verified requirement — the traceability matrix, generated. A capability validated in use — the frozen-section program, measured over nearly three thousand frozen sections; Dialogue is not here yet, and I say so. And the fifth rung, patients did better, which is empty for all four and stays empty until someone measures it. The conclusion is not that AI is unreliable so be careful. It is that faster construction makes explicit requirements, expert review and good tests more valuable, not less — and this ladder is how you say which claim you are making.

takeaway.text: Faster construction makes explicit requirements, expert review and good tests more valuable, not less.
takeaway.comment: The shape is the evidence ladder from the operating-system talk, turned on software we built ourselves rather than on published models. “The data has the right shape” is the bottom rung; “patients did better” is the top, and it is empty for all four systems until someone measures it. Faster construction lowers the cost of every rung except the ones that need a person who knows the domain: deciding what the requirement should be, and defining the intended use against which the system is validated.

slides.title: Where the Pathologist's Knowledge Enters the System
slides.subtitle: One requirement from each system — the sentence only a domain expert could have written
numberedItems: Dialogue — ignore differences in wording that do not change the diagnosis; raise the ones that change side, site, identity or specimen.
Hedgehog — a handoff is complete only when the receiving party acknowledges it; an open handoff stays visible to both ends until then.
IBIS — show the interpretation and the generated query, and wait for approval before anything executes; the unit of the result is stated, not assumed.
WBC ΔΣ — completing a count below the target is never blocked; the report carries the count, the target, and the confidence interval that count supports.
Frozen-section QA — every frozen-section diagnosis is scored at sign-out as agree, margin assurance, defer, or disagree with a reason; after six months, a hard stop.
slides.speakerNotes: One sentence per system, and in every case it is the sentence the software could not have written for itself. Which differences to ignore. When a handoff is complete. What must be shown before a query runs. What happens when a count stops early. How a frozen section is scored. Requirements are patient safety made explicit, and they are the part of this work that belongs to the people in this room. The first one is my paraphrase of how the tool is described, not a quotation from a written requirement; if you have the real sentence, use it. The WBC ΔΣ requirement is from the current README; the FSQA scoring categories are from the AJCP 2025 paper.

takeaway.text: This is what AI cannot invent for you. Only domain experts can write the requirement that protects a patient.
takeaway.comment: Five sentences, one per system, and each is the sentence the software could not have written for itself: which differences to ignore, when a handoff is complete, what must be shown before a query runs, what happens when a count stops early, how a frozen section is scored. The counter’s rule is from its published requirements, the frozen-section categories from the 2025 paper, the Dialogue sentence a paraphrase of the tool’s published description. Requirements are patient safety made explicit.

slides.speakerNotes: Two models I reject, struck through on either side. Everyone becomes a programmer: unsupported tools, verification theater, drift, security by enthusiasm. We no longer need engineering: untestable requirements, a model that proposes mistaken for a system that is accountable, nobody owning the artifact after the demo. The one in the middle is the one that has worked here for twenty years and now works faster: pathologists contribute the intended behavior, the meaningful exceptions and the acceptance criteria; an accountable team turns those into supported infrastructure. The loop at the bottom is the whole talk: intent, specification, build, test, use, revised intent. If the department chair is in the room, this is the slide to pause on.

takeaway.text: Neither 'everyone should become a programmer' nor 'we no longer need engineering'. Clinically led, informatics enabled.
takeaway.comment: The earlier research talk argued for the team’s existence; this slide argues the division of labor inside it. The pathologist owns the intended behavior, the exceptions and the evidence that would convince them. The accountable team owns the perimeter, the verification, the change record and the artifact after the demo — and is the only one of the three models that can answer a request with “not yet, sharpen the question”.

slides.title: The Safety Boundary, Across All Four Systems

left.heading: AI Does (Development Partner, and Proposer)
bullets: Turns stated intent into requirements, scaffolds, tests and documentation — Hedgehog, WBC ΔΣ, IBIS, this deck
Compares documents and proposes flags with its rationale — Dialogue, before release
Translates a question into an inspectable query — IBIS, before execution
Generates the adversarial test records — Xenonym
Drafts the quality documents, and the checks that keep them honest

right.heading: AI Must Not (Non-Negotiable)
bullets: Decide. No autonomous clinical decision: a flag is accepted or dismissed by a pathologist; a count is made by a technologist
See PHI in prompts. Built outside the institution on synthetic data; brought inside along the governed pathway
Make hidden transformations. Every filter, join, recode and flag is testable and reviewable
Ship unverified. Reviewed, tested against the shipped code, traced to a requirement
Be the memory. Sessions forget; the executable quality system remembers

slides.speakerNotes: Read both columns aloud; the non-negotiables matter as much as the capabilities. The left column is what the four systems let AI do: construct, propose, translate, generate, draft. The right column is what none of them lets it do: decide, see PHI, transform silently, ship unverified — and the fifth, which this talk adds to the earlier lectures' list: be the memory. Sessions forget. The executable quality system remembers.

takeaway.text: AI is a development partner and, inside Dialogue, a proposer. It is never the decider — and never the memory.
takeaway.comment: The first four non-negotiables are the ones the residents’ lecture and the research talk set out. The fifth — never the memory — is the counter’s lesson: a session that can be told anything cannot be relied on to remember what it was told, so what the system must do has to live outside the model, in requirements and in checks that fail the build. It is the one most teams adopting AI-assisted development have not yet learned.

slides.title: Key Takeaways
items: Pathologists are becoming designers of how pathology works. The 2016 prediction aimed at judgment and missed context. The distance between recognizing what should happen and having infrastructure that makes it happen was never intellectual; it was the cost of implementation, and that cost has collapsed.

Two kinds of AI, kept separate. AI inside the application proposes and needs task-appropriate evaluation; AI helping construct the application leaves no model in the loop. The most valuable built systems often should behave predictably.

A correct diagnosis is not a coherent clinical record. Dialogue extends clinical attention over the relationships that make a diagnosis usable — and which contradictions matter is a pathology question.
Infrastructure changes practice; say what the evidence is. Seventy days to eight is a workflow result. AI changes how fast such infrastructure can be built, tested and revised.

Faster construction makes requirements, review and tests more valuable, not less — and a quality system protects no one until it is executable. A green build that executes nothing is the failure mode AI makes cheap.

Sit C, Srinivasan R, Amlani A, et al. Attitudes and perceptions of UK medical students towards artificial intelligence and radiology: a multicentre survey. Insights Imaging. 2020;11:14. 484 responses, 19 schools; 49% less likely to consider radiology because of AI.

Reeder K, Lee H. Impact of artificial intelligence on US medical students’ choice of radiology. Clin Imaging. 2022;81:67-71. 32 schools; one-sixth of would-be first-choice students did not choose radiology because of AI.

The Clinical Anchor — Dialogue and Amended Reports

Corcoran TP. Yale Pathology develops AI tool that checks records to ensure accuracy. Yale School of Medicine news, 23 Oct 2025. Concept: Gershkovich and Gibson; built by Celano. The breast-biopsy laterality catch; one click before sign-out; feedback and rating; no performance figures.

Parkash V, Domfeh A, Cohen P, Fischbach N, Pronovost M, Haines GK, Gershkovich P. Are amended surgical pathology reports getting to the correct responsible care provider? Am J Clin Pathol. 2014;142(1):58-63. 60 amended reports; 7 ordering/treating discrepancies, all malignant; the amendment in the treating chart in 1 of 7.

Friedman CP. A “fundamental theorem” of biomedical informatics. JAMIA. 2009;16(2):169-170.

The Operational Anchor — Custody and Frozen-Section QA

Gibson JA, Mutnick N, Gershkovich P, Sinard J. Software solution for integration of frozen section quality assurance into daily practice. Am J Clin Pathol. 2025;163(5):794-802. 70 to 8 days; 35% to 75%; 3.2% to 2.2% not significant; 2,960 frozen sections in 1,805 cases after go-live in October 2022.

Gershkovich P, Sinard JH. Customizing laboratory information systems: closing the functionality gap. Adv Anat Pathol. 2015;22(5):323-330. · Sinard JH, Gershkovich P. Custom software development for use in a clinical laboratory. J Pathol Inform. 2012;3:44.

Hedgehog, FSLink, POinT, RTSE, Histology Asset Tracking, Pathology Portal, RELAY: Yale Pathology Informatics systems described in the presenter's curriculum vitae (November 2025). No usage statistics for Hedgehog are published; the custody requirement on the slide is an illustrative formulation.

McQuade JM, Murray RM (co-chairs). Software Is Never Done. Defense Innovation Board, 2019.

The Research Anchor — IBIS

IBIS — Interactive Biomedical Inquiry System. OpenPathologyFoundation/ibis (repository not yet public). Natural language to Lucene with interpretation, confidence, entities and a confirmation step; 200 synthetic seed cases. Field names on the demo slide are illustrative.

How Do We Know It Works — WBC ΔΣ and Xenonym

WBC ΔΣ — Manual Differential Counter. OpenPathologyFoundation/tessera. · mdc.openpathology.org README v2.24.0 (23 Aug 2026), generated facts: 1,172 tests (722 Node + 450 browser), 71 URS, 207 SRS, 56 hazards, 803 verification cases, 100% traceability. QMS/DHF/DCR/DCR-004 (4 Aug 2026): the 379-test baseline that executed nothing and the fourteen defects behind it. QMS/DHF/DRIFT-LOG.md: 52 incidents, 42 prevented, append-only. TR-001 v4.2 records 191 tests at the same baseline; the discrepancy is noted in REFERENCES.md.

Xenonym — synthetic patient and professional data generator. OpenPathologyFoundation/xenonym (repository not yet public). · xenonym.openpathology.org Realistic and stress modes; JSON, CSV and FHIR R4; schema-driven output. No cross-record consistency feature, and none is claimed.

Documented Harm and the Scale of Identification Error

The Joint Commission, sentinel event annual review of 2024 (released 9 Jul 2025), as reported by Periop Leader. 1,575 events; 127 wrong-surgery events, up 13%; 68% wrong-site, laterality cited in over half; 51% severe temporary and 36% permanent harm.

Makary MA, Epstein J, Pronovost PJ, et al. Surgical specimen identification errors: a new measure of quality in surgical care. Surgery. 2007;141(4):450-455. 91 of 21,351 specimens; 4.3 per 1,000. · Nakhleh RE, Idowu MO, Souers RJ, et al. Mislabeling of cases, specimens, blocks, and slides: a CAP study of 136 institutions. Arch Pathol Lab Med. 2011;135(8):969-974. 0.11% cumulative.

Pfeifer JD, Liu J. Rate of occult specimen provenance complications in routine clinical practice. Am J Clin Pathol. 2013;139(1):93-100. About 13,000 prostate biopsies, 54 practices; 0.26% switched, 0.67% contaminated. Data supplied by Strand Analytical Laboratories, which markets the test. · Dunn EJ, Moga PJ. Patient misidentification in laboratory medicine: a qualitative analysis of 227 root cause analysis reports in the Veterans Health Administration. Arch Pathol Lab Med. 2010;134(2):244-255. 182 of 253 adverse events.

Reason J. Human error: models and management. BMJ. 2000;320(7237):768-770. The Swiss cheese model; the slide paraphrases. · Gertz RJ, et al. Potential of GPT-4 for detecting errors in radiology reports. Radiology. 2024; doi:10.1148/radiol.232714 (RSNA release). 150 inserted errors in 100 of 200 reports; GPT-4 82.7%, senior radiologists 89.3%, attendings and residents 80.0%.

The six cases: Eason, Long Island (Medical News Today, 4 Oct 2007) · Methodist Hospital, St. Louis Park (MPR News, 18 Mar 2008) · Barros and Cloutman, Boston (Lubin & Meyer, 2 Aug 2010) · Craven, New Haven (NBC Connecticut, 17 Mar 2016) · Barksdale, Georgia (AP via Fortune, 8 Aug 2026; allegations in a lawsuit) · Jacks, Marietta (NBC Connecticut, 30 Sep 2026).

Operating Model and Governance

Hart SN, Hoffman NG, Gershkovich P, et al. Organizational preparedness for the use of large language models in pathology informatics. J Pathol Inform. 2023;14:100338.

Gershkovich P. Wearing a fur coat in the summertime: should digital pathology redefine medical imaging? J Pathol Inform. 2025;18:100450. The behavioral-interoperability argument.

Lincoln TL, Korpman RA. Computers, health care, and medical information science. Science. 1980;210(4467):257-263. Attributed as paraphrase; the sentences sometimes quoted from it could not be verified in the abstract.

CAP. AI tools make predictions, pathologists make diagnoses. September 2025. · Anthropic. Claude Code best practices: explore, plan, implement, verify.
